newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government faces week of strikes.
newsitem.headline: French government faces week of strikes.

text.p: France faces a week of protests against government cutbacks and record unemployment which will culminate in a 24-hour strike by civil servants, teachers, rail and gas workers on Thursday.

With more than three million people out of work and tens of thousands more to lose their jobs through public spending cuts, Thursday's strike should show if the will is there for the kind of showdown which crippled the country late last year.

The question is whether the protest will generate a turnout on a scale that could upset Prime Minister Alain Juppe's drive to trim public spending and the civil service in preparation for a single European currency.
Unions and some government back-benchers say his policy is hurting the economy and jobs as a result.

Unlike last year, when railworkers protesting against a threat to their early pension rights spearheaded a 24-day public sector strike against welfare reforms, turf battles in the past few months have strained trade union unity.

Nicole Notat, head of the largest trade union, the CFDT, said the protests were the result of "indignation" and that the government should be attacking unemployment to help the economy, not hoping the economy would pick up and help employment.
"Things just can't go on like this," she said on Saturday. "It's unemployment that's dragging the economy down."
Marc Blondel, general secretary of the Force Ouvriere union, said all the ingredients were in place for a social explosion but no one could tell when it would happen.

"In 1974 there were 400,000 unemployed, now there are 3.2 million. It's no longer a transitory crisis between two periods. We're talking about a sea change in society. Things are going to explode," Blondel said.
The main cause of Thursday's strike is a plan in the 1997 budget to trim the civil service by nearly 6,000.
Education will bear the brunt of job cuts seen as the thin end of the wedge, with a loss of 2,300 permanent posts in 1997 and the layoff of some 15,000 teachers on short-term contracts.
All the main civil service unions have joined the strike, including local and national administrations and hospital staff.
Unions representing teachers, railwaymen, gas and electricity workers have all joined the stoppage.
Pilots at Air France Europe, the national carrier's domestic and European subsidiary, have said they will join the action and there could be disruption on the Paris bus and Metro network.
The warm-up for Thursday comes from journalists, defence workers and possible early disruption at Air France Europe.

Thousands demonstrated in Paris on Saturday against defence cuts that will axe 8,000 jobs at firms such as planemaker Aerospatiale and arms manufacturer GIAT. A recent parliamentary report forecast 50,000-75,000 eventual job losses in the sector.

Journalists' unions have called a strike for Tuesday over government plans to scrap an income tax deduction introduced in 1934 to compensate for professional expenses. Single journalists on an average salary will have to pay some 30 percent more tax.
Since last year's strike, the government has dropped plans to change railworkers' early pension rights and promised to relieve the SNCF state railways of massive debts.
But the unions are worried about job losses and fear that a reform splitting SNCF's transport operations and infrastructure could prepare it for privatisation one day.

Discontent with Juppe was dramatised by a parliamentary by-election in the Marseille suburb of Gardanne on Sunday in which the government-backed candidate came a distant third, leaving a run-off between a Communist and the extreme-right National Front, both of which oppose European monetary union.
